title: Short Stuff: Mood Rings
summary: Short Stuff episode on mood rings. The hosts recall their 1970s popularity (about forty million sold after the 1975 fad) and discuss the inventors often credited: Maris Ambats and Josh Reynolds, who reportedly launched the ring in 1975 through a company called Q-Tran, and jeweler Marvin Wernick, who reportedly got the idea from a doctor using thermotropic tape on a child's forehead. Neither got a patent in time, and a Chinese inventor patented the design in 1997. The hosts then explain the science: thermotropic liquid crystals twist with temperature and reflect different colors, and skin temperature shifts with mood. The color scale runs from green (normal) through blue (relaxed, then passionate or happy) to amber, gray, and black (anxious to very stressed). They conclude mood rings work in a loose sense, since they track skin temperature, not emotion directly.

segments.title: Opening banter and topic intro
segments.summary: The hosts open the short episode and introduce mood rings as a bite-size topic, citing HowStuffWorks, the Chicago Tribune, and Atlas Obscura as sources.

segments.title: 1975 fad and inventor claims
segments.summary: The hosts describe the mid-1970s mood ring craze, with about forty million sold. They discuss Maris Ambats and Josh Reynolds, who are most often credited as inventors and who reportedly launched the ring through Q-Tran Ltd as a biofeedback-themed venture.

segments.title: Marvin Wernick and the missing patent
segments.summary: The hosts discuss jeweler Marvin Wernick, who reportedly got the idea after seeing a doctor use thermotropic tape to read a child's temperature. Neither Reynolds nor Wernick patented the ring before the fad ended.

segments.title: 1997 patent and 1990s fashion tangent
segments.summary: The hosts note a Chinese inventor who patented the mood ring in 1997, then digress into 1990s fashion, including parachute pants and factory-second clothing stores.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break in the conversation, with a quick Gucci and Polo joke.

segments.title: Mood jewelry variants and do they work
segments.summary: The hosts describe mood pendants, chokers, and bracelets, later called biomood or truth jewelry, and set up the question of whether mood rings work.

segments.title: The science of mood ring color changes
segments.summary: The hosts explain that a mood ring holds thermotropic liquid crystals in a glass container. The crystals twist with temperature and reflect different light colors. Skin temperature changes with mood, so the ring is loosely real, not magic or bunk.

segments.title: Mood ring color scale and verdict
segments.summary: The hosts walk through the color meanings: green for normal, blue for relaxed then passionate or happy, and amber, gray, and black for increasing anxiety and stress. They agree the rings only partly track emotion and conclude they kind of work.

segments.title: Verdict and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck gives the verdict that mood rings kind of work, which means the episode is a Short Stuff. The show's production credit closes the episode.
